stories.headline: Aurora Police Officer Indicted on Murder, Manslaughter Charges in 2025 Traffic Stop Shooting
stories.summary:
A grand jury has indicted Aurora police officer Matthew Neely, 54, on charges of second-degree murder and manslaughter in the August 2025 shooting death of Rajon Belt-Stubblefield, a 37-year-old Black man. The indictment, filed Friday and unsealed Monday, alleges Neely shot Belt-Stubblefield following a traffic stop near East Sixth Avenue and Sable Boulevard after Belt-Stubblefield fled, crashed, and then exited his vehicle.

According to the indictment, Belt-Stubblefield threw a gun to the ground before the confrontation escalated physically. After Belt-Stubblefield assumed a fighting stance and advanced toward Neely, the officer shot him. The indictment notes Neely spent seven seconds attempting to holster his firearm to deploy a less-lethal weapon but was unsuccessful; he was not carrying a Taser.

The case is among the most significant police-involved shooting prosecutions in Aurora's recent history. Belt-Stubblefield's son, Zion Murphy, was present at the scene during the confrontation, according to the indictment.

stories.headline: Denver City Council Rejects 4 A.M. Club Closing Time, Approves Sweeping Nightlife Safety Rules
stories.summary:
Denver City Council voted 12-1 Monday to reject a proposal that would have allowed nightclubs to remain open until 4 a.m., though alcohol sales would still have been capped at 2 a.m. under state law. Councilwoman Jamie Torres, who introduced the amendment removing the 4 a.m. provision, said she was not yet comfortable with the data supporting the idea, though she left the door open to a future pilot program in select areas of the city.

The council did approve the broader nightlife licensing ordinance, also 12-1, which overhauls a regulatory framework that had not been updated since the 1980s. The new rules consolidate 14 license types into three categories, require mandatory surveillance cameras and security plans, and prohibit weapons at nightclubs.

The vote came after the council delayed action in July following a deadly shooting at Ultra Lounge East in southeast Denver that left one person dead and eight injured. That club has since permanently closed after the city suspended its licenses. Councilwoman Flor Alvidrez cast the lone dissenting vote on the final ordinance, citing concerns from businesses about new liability exposure.

stories.headline: Gun Background Checks in Colorado Nearly Triple in July as New Semiautomatic Rifle Law Takes Effect
stories.summary:
The Colorado Bureau of Investigation processed a record 59,452 firearm background check requests in July, nearly triple the 20,172 processed in the same month last year, as residents rushed to purchase semiautomatic weapons ahead of a new state law that took effect Saturday. Senate Bill 3, passed by the Democratic-controlled legislature in 2025, requires buyers of many semiautomatic firearms with detachable magazines — including AR-15-style rifles — to complete a multi-day safety course and undergo an enhanced background check through their county sheriff.

The process can cost hundreds of dollars. Colorado Parks and Wildlife developed the mandatory curriculum with 11 volunteer firearms instructors and covers topics including safe storage, mental illness and firearms, extreme risk protection orders, and victim awareness. CBI added staff and implemented flexible scheduling to meet the surge, successfully processing all checks within the 72-hour window required by state law.

State Sen. Tom Sullivan, the Centennial Democrat who sponsored the bill, described the measure as effectively a ban on assault weapons. The law represents one of the most restrictive gun purchase requirements ever enacted in Colorado.

stories.headline: Colorado Democrats Shift on Israel Aid, Reflecting Growing Divide Within the Party
stories.summary:
All of Colorado's Democratic U.S. House members voted for a Republican-sponsored amendment to strip foreign aid to Israel from a State Department appropriations bill, marking a dramatic reversal from two years ago when every Colorado Democrat voted to provide such aid. The shift came as nearly half the House Democratic caucus joined the vote, a sign of deepening tensions over U.S. policy toward Israel following the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas attacks and Israel's subsequent military campaign in Gaza.

The political change has real electoral consequences in Colorado. In Denver's 1st Congressional District, long-time incumbent Diana DeGette lost her Democratic primary to democratic socialist Melat Kiros, who had previously been fired from her law job over a post about Israel's actions in Gaza. Voters cited Gaza policy as a driving factor in that race.

University of Denver political science professor Seth Masket said the shift is largely generational, driven by younger Democrats who associate Israel primarily with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Rep. Brittany Pettersen of Lakewood framed her vote as a message to Netanyahu rather than a withdrawal of support for the Israeli people, while Rep. Joe Neguse of Lafayette described the party as a "big tent" with a wide range of foreign policy views.

stories.headline: Denver Council Members Seek Guardrails on Parking Meter Fund After City Stretches Spending Intent
stories.summary:
Two Denver City Council members are pushing new restrictions on how the city spends revenue from its parking meter fund, arguing the Johnston administration has used the money for purposes beyond the fund's original transportation and mobility mission. Councilwomen Flor Alvidrez and Shontel Lewis introduced a draft proposal that would codify exactly which programs can be funded by the Transportation and Mobility Special Revenue Fund, which collects proceeds from a $1-per-hour meter rate increase enacted in 2021.

The fund is expected to generate $12.5 million in 2027. Alvidrez cited examples including $200,000 spent to replace downtown bike lane posts with raised dividers and $8.75 million budgeted for parking enforcement and management software — including a new ticket appeals system — as uses that stretch the fund's intent. "Parking isn't mobility," Alvidrez said.

The city's Department of Transportation and Infrastructure defended the expenditures as consistent with the ordinance's broad language and said the changes went through the council budget process transparently. The proposal follows a spike in Denver traffic deaths last year and comes amid ongoing debate over the city's transportation priorities.

stories.headline: Artemis II Astronauts Draw Sellout Crowd of 9,500 at Red Rocks Amphitheatre
stories.summary:
The four astronauts of NASA's Artemis II mission — commander Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, and mission specialists Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen — appeared before a sellout crowd of more than 9,500 people at Red Rocks Amphitheatre in Morrison on Monday morning. The crew, who in April became the first humans in history to travel to the far side of the moon, walked the audience through their nine-day mission using photos and videos.

Parking lots were already filling before the venue's doors opened, and lines wound down the amphitheater's stairs and ramps. Children lined up at a shortened microphone to ask the astronauts questions, and Koch described how from near the moon, the Earth appeared not fragile but powerful — "a lifeboat, an oasis hanging in the universe."

The event was part of a public outreach tour following the April mission. Koch noted that the goal of the mission was always to inspire people, and she and her crewmates shared personal moments from the journey, including adjusting back to Earth's gravity after spending days in space.

stories.headline: Xcel Energy Begins Burying 50 Miles of Power Lines in Colorado to Reduce Wildfire Risk
stories.summary:
Xcel Energy has begun construction on a plan to bury approximately 50 miles of overhead power lines across Colorado by 2027 as part of a $1.9 billion wildfire mitigation program approved by the Colorado Public Utilities Commission. Work began with a 1.7-mile stretch along 75th Street in Boulder County, an area still scarred by the Marshall Fire, which destroyed more than 1,000 homes and remains the costliest wildfire in Colorado history.

The undergrounding effort is a response to years of community pressure following frustration with Xcel's Public Safety Power Shutoffs, which left thousands of customers without electricity for days during high fire-risk weather events. Xcel Colorado president Robert Kenney said the company is targeting locations where wildfire risk is highest and where soil conditions make undergrounding feasible.

The program also includes expanded vegetation management and installation of additional weather-monitoring and AI-enabled cameras to detect fires earlier. Kenney said Xcel plans to file another multi-year wildfire mitigation plan with the PUC in 2027, though he noted regulatory red tape is slowing longer-term expansion of the project. Costs will be recovered through customer rates approved by the PUC.

stories.headline: Colorado Wildfire Smoke Returns, Health Advisories Issued Across Northern and Western Counties
stories.summary:
Wildfire smoke from fires in Nevada, Utah, and the Pacific Northwest has returned to Colorado after several weeks of relatively clean air, prompting air quality health advisories for Boulder, Grand, Jackson, Larimer, Moffat, Rio Blanco, and Routt counties through at least Tuesday morning. Air quality index readings in communities including Steamboat Springs, Craig, Kremmling, and Granby ranged from 110 to 130 — classified as "unhealthy for sensitive groups" — on Monday.

Colorado health officials warned that wind patterns could cause conditions to shift rapidly and that an additional dose of smoke could arrive Monday afternoon and evening from the northwest. Five large wildfires were actively burning in Colorado as of Monday, including the Aspen Acres Fire in Custer County at approximately 102,000 acres and 67 percent containment, and the Gold Mountain Fire near Ouray at 39,500 acres and 72 percent containment.

Nationally, more than 35,000 wildfires have burned approximately 3.75 million acres this year — roughly 130 percent above the 10-year average — according to the National Interagency Fire Center. Scientists have linked the worsening fire seasons to climate-driven warmer and drier conditions across the West.

stories.headline: Man Dies in Boating Incident at Monument Lake Resort in Southern Colorado
stories.summary:
Colorado Parks and Wildlife officers recovered the body of a man Monday evening after he went missing during a boating incident at Monument Lake Resort in Las Animas County, approximately 40 miles west of Trinidad. The man was among four family members aboard a pontoon boat when the incident occurred. The three surviving family members — two adults and a child — were transported to Mt. San Rafael Hospital in Trinidad.

CPW received the initial report at 10:15 a.m. and deployed boats equipped with side-scanning sonar and an underwater remotely operated vehicle to search the lake. The victim was located in approximately 17 feet of water at around 5:15 p.m. His identity was not immediately released, and the Las Animas County Coroner will determine the cause and manner of death.

Monument Lake Resort, founded in 1937 and situated on 368 acres in the Sangre de Cristo range near the New Mexico border, is a private resort known for its adobe architecture. The search was conducted jointly by CPW, the Las Animas County Sheriff's Office, and Las Animas County Emergency Management.

stories.headline: Colorado Pharmacy Board Sues Denver Restaurant for Selling Antibiotics Without a License
stories.summary:
The Colorado State Board of Pharmacy has filed a lawsuit against Panaderia y Taqueria Chihuas, a restaurant and bakery at 4810 Chambers Road in Denver's Gateway neighborhood, for allegedly selling prescription antibiotics without a license. The lawsuit, filed July 9, alleges the business violated a cease-and-desist order the board issued in February after an anonymous complaint reported the restaurant was selling antibiotics imported from Mexico.

An undercover investigator purchased the anti-parasitic drug mebendazole at the establishment in February. A follow-up visit in late March, after the cease-and-desist order was in place, found the restaurant was still selling oxytetracycline/polymyxin B, a topical antibiotic used for eye infections. Neither drug has recreational use, though mebendazole's name-brand equivalent can cost more than $4,000 for a course, making imported versions attractive to price-conscious consumers.

The case is described as uncommon by pharmacy board officials. A comparable recent case involved a restaurant in Meeker that dispensed antibiotics and cough medicines, but that matter was resolved with a cease-and-desist order alone. Representatives for the restaurant did not respond to media inquiries.

stories.headline: Aurora Apartment Fire Displaces 50 Residents, Damages 24 Units
stories.summary:
A two-alarm fire broke out Monday afternoon at a three-story apartment building in the 16200 block of East Alameda Place in Aurora, displacing 50 residents from 24 apartments. Firefighters battled flames visible in the building's attic before extinguishing the fire by late afternoon. One person was evaluated by paramedics but did not require hospitalization, and two cats were treated with oxygen.

Aurora Fire Rescue and Aurora Police Department responded to the scene. The American Red Cross was called to assist displaced residents and their pets. Firefighters remained on scene into the evening to address hot spots.

The cause of the fire was not immediately announced. No additional injuries were reported.

stories.headline: Rio Blanco Fire Near Pagosa Springs Grows to Over 1,000 Acres, Threatens 827 Homes; Reservoir Closed for Air Operations
stories.summary:
The Rio Blanco Fire south of Pagosa Springs has grown to more than 1,082 acres with only 11 percent containment as of Monday, threatening an estimated 827 homes since it was first discovered July 28. Colorado Parks and Wildlife has temporarily closed boating access at Echo Canyon Reservoir, about four miles south of Pagosa Springs, to allow aircraft to safely scoop water for aerial firefighting operations.

Hiking and shore fishing at the reservoir remain permitted. CPW Area Wildlife Manager Adrian Archuleta said the closure applies to all watercraft, including kayaks, canoes, and paddleboards, to protect the safety of air support operations. The reservoir sits off U.S. Highway 84 and spans 211 acres.

The Rio Blanco Fire is one of five large wildfires currently burning in Colorado. The fire's growth comes amid a statewide wildfire season that has already seen multiple large blazes, a prolonged drought, and record-low streamflows across the state.

topStory.headline: Arson Suspect Arrested as Wildfires Destroy More Than 700 Structures, Displace 65,000 Near Spokane
topStory.summary:
A 37-year-old Spokane man has been arrested and charged with first-degree arson in connection with one of three major wildfires burning in Spokane County, Washington, officials announced Monday. Aaron Farinacci was taken into custody after witnesses reported seeing him kneeling near grass at the site of the Old Trails Fire, and he was later found carrying matches and a lighter, according to Spokane County Sheriff John Nowels. Farinacci, who has a prior manslaughter conviction, is being held on $1 million bond.

The three fires — identified as Old Trails, Fairview and Autumn Lane — have collectively burned more than 8,000 acres since igniting Saturday, destroying more than 700 structures and forcing the evacuation of nearly 65,000 residents from the Spokane area. No deaths or injuries have been confirmed, though authorities are still attempting to contact 14 people who have not responded to outreach. Officials said those individuals are not considered missing and may simply have dead phone batteries or have already reached safety.

Washington Governor Bob Ferguson called the situation a "nightmare" and described it as likely the worst natural disaster in Spokane's history. Ferguson told CNN that the arson arrest added to the "absolute anguish" of those who lost their homes, saying it made "a tragic situation more heartbreaking" to consider that much of the damage may have been deliberately set. Spokane Mayor Lisa Brown warned there remained "the potential for lives to be lost" and said it was too early to say when evacuees could return home.

More than 900 firefighters are currently assigned to the Washington fires, with reinforcements expected from other states. Cooler temperatures and lighter winds were forecast for Tuesday, offering crews a brief window to make progress, but temperatures are expected to climb back into the 90s later in the week. Governor Ferguson has issued a statewide ban on all outdoor fires. The blazes near Spokane are among 17 major wildfires burning across Washington state, while neighboring Oregon has seen more than 2 million acres burn this season — shattering that state's previous wildfire record — in what officials describe as the worst regional fire season in more than 30 years.
